2027-05-16.title: Pentecost Sunday
readings: All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages
Lord, send forth your Spirit, and renew the face of the earth (or: Alleluia)
In the one Spirit we were all baptized into one body
Come, Holy Spirit (the Sequence is obligatory today and is sung before the Alleluia)
As the Father has sent me, so I send you. Receive the Holy Spirit
2027-05-16.alt: Solemnity, Mass during the Day, Year B. Gloria, Sequence and Creed. In place of the second reading Galatians 5:16–25 may be read, and in place of the Gospel John 15:26–27; 16:12–15. Today the fifty days of Easter come to their close: at the dismissal the double Alleluia is sung for the last time, and after Evening Prayer the paschal candle is moved to the baptistery, where it will be lit at baptisms and beside the coffin at funerals. From tomorrow the Angelus replaces the Regina Caeli, and Ordinary Time resumes. Liturgical colour: red.
2027-05-16.verse: All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages, as the Spirit gave them ability.
theo: “When the day of Pentecost had come, they were all together in one place.” Pentecost was not a new feast invented by the Church. It was one of the three great pilgrim feasts of Israel, Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks, kept fifty days after Passover (the Greek word pentēkostē means “fiftieth”). It began as a harvest festival, when the first loaves of the new wheat were offered to God (Leviticus 23:16); in the time of Jesus many also linked it with the gift of the Law at Sinai, which came about fifty days after the Exodus. That is why Jerusalem is full of “devout Jews from every nation under heaven.” And now, fifty days after the Passover of Jesus' death and resurrection, God gives the first harvest of the new creation and a new law, written not on stone but on hearts. The signs recall Sinai, where “the Lord had descended upon it in fire” with thunder and a trumpet blast: “suddenly from heaven there came a sound like the rush of a violent wind, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting. Divided tongues, as of fire, appeared among them, and a tongue rested on each of them.” Wind and breath are one word in Hebrew (ruach) and in Greek (pneuma); John the Baptist had promised one who would baptise “with the Holy Spirit and fire.” Then the gift is named: “All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages, as the Spirit gave them ability.”

The crowd that gathers is astonished: “Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how is it that we hear, each of us, in our own native language?” Luke lists the nations, from Parthians and Medes in the east to visitors from Rome in the west, Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabs. The Fathers of the Church saw here the reversal of Babel. At Babel people tried to build “a tower with its top in the heavens” and “make a name for ourselves,” and they ended unable to understand one another, scattered over the earth (Genesis 11). At Pentecost God comes down as a gift, and the scattered are gathered: not by forcing everyone into one language, but by making the one Gospel heard in every language. The Church is born speaking many tongues. Here, in a land of many languages, we can feel the meaning of this: the same Good News is proclaimed today in Malayalam and Tamil, Hindi and Konkani, Telugu and Kannada and English, and it is one faith. What they all hear is the same: “in our own languages we hear them speaking about God's deeds of power.” The Psalm sings the Spirit's work on all creation: “When you send forth your spirit, they are created; and you renew the face of the ground.” The Lectionary refrain prays it as a petition: Lord, send forth your Spirit, and renew the face of the earth.

St Paul, writing to a quarrelsome community in Corinth, shows us the Spirit's work inside the Church. First, faith itself is his gift: “no one can say ‘Jesus is Lord’ except by the Holy Spirit.” Every act of faith, every prayer, even the simplest “Jesus,” is already the Spirit at work in us. Then he speaks of variety in unity: “there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of services, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who activates all of them in everyone.” Spirit, Lord, God: Paul names the whole Trinity in one breath. And the purpose of every gift is clear: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.” Gifts are not medals for display but tools for building up others. Finally the image of the body: “For in the one Spirit we were all baptized into one body,” and “we were all made to drink of one Spirit.” Baptism plunged us into the Spirit; Confirmation sealed us with him; the Eucharist makes us one body. If the second reading from Galatians is chosen, Paul lists “the fruit of the Spirit”: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, generosity, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control.” These are the signs that the Spirit lives in us.

The Gospel takes us back to the evening of Easter Day. The disciples are behind locked doors “for fear of the Jews,” which in John's Gospel means the Temple authorities who had handed Jesus over, not the Jewish people as such; the disciples themselves were Jews. Jesus comes and stands among them: “Peace be with you.” He shows them his hands and his side, the wounds that are now the proof of his love and his victory. Then he sends them: “As the Father has sent me, so I send you.” And “he breathed on them and said to them, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit.’” The verb John uses for “breathed” is the same word the Greek Bible uses in Genesis, when the Lord God “breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and the man became a living being.” The risen Christ breathes a new creation into his disciples. And the first work of that new creation is forgiveness: “If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained.” The Church has always heard in these words the institution of the sacrament of Penance: the Holy Spirit is given for the forgiveness of sins. If the alternative Gospel is read, Jesus promises “the Advocate … the Spirit of truth,” who “will guide you into all the truth.”

Luke tells us who was in the upper room when the Spirit came: the apostles, “together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14). The one who conceived the Son of God by the power of the Holy Spirit was there when the same Spirit came upon the Church. Mary prayed with the apostles for the gift she had already received in fullness; she is the Mother of the Church at its birth, and tomorrow the Church will honour her with that title. Today the Church prays the ancient Sequence, Veni, Sancte Spiritus, with its tender names for the Spirit: Father of the poor, giver of gifts, light of hearts, best of comforters, sweet guest of the soul, rest in labour, coolness in the heat, comfort in tears. It asks him to wash what is stained, water what is dry, heal what is wounded, bend what is rigid, warm what is cold, and guide what has gone astray. That is the prayer for every Christian today. The Easter season ends not with an ending but with a sending. The candle that stood by the ambo for fifty days goes to the font, because the fire of Easter now burns in the baptised, sent out into the world with the Spirit's peace.
conn: Pentecost (pentēkostē).

Greek for “fiftieth.” In Israel, Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks (Exodus 34:22; Leviticus 23:15–21; Deuteronomy 16:9–12), seven weeks after Passover. A pilgrim feast, which is why Jerusalem was crowded with Jews from many lands.
Wind and fire.
Hebrew ruach and Greek pneuma mean wind, breath and spirit. Fire recalls the burning bush (Exodus 3:2), the pillar of fire, and Sinai wrapped in smoke and fire (Exodus 19:18).
Babel reversed.

Genesis 11:1–9: proud builders end in confusion and scattering. Acts 2: a gift from above brings understanding and gathering. Many Fathers, among them St Cyril of Jerusalem and St Augustine, made this connection.
The list of nations.

Fifteen peoples, from Persia (Parthians, Medes, Elamites) to Rome, and from Crete to Arabia. Luke paints the whole known world gathered in Jerusalem, a preview of the Gospel's journey “to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8).
“Jesus is Lord.”

Perhaps the earliest Christian creed. Kyrios, Lord, was the word the Greek Bible used for the divine name of God. To call Jesus Lord is to confess his divinity, which no one can do except by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3).
Charisms.

Paul's word charismata means gifts of grace. He lists many: wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, discernment, tongues and their interpretation (1 Corinthians 12:8–10). All are “for the common good.”
“For fear of the Jews.”

In John's Gospel “the Jews” often means the religious authorities in Jerusalem who opposed Jesus. The Church teaches that the Jewish people as a whole, then or now, cannot be blamed for his death (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 597–598).
He breathed on them.
The Greek emphysaō appears in Genesis 2:7 (God breathes life into Adam), Ezekiel 37:9 (breath enters the dry bones) and Wisdom 15:11. In John 20:22 the risen Jesus does what only the Creator does.
Forgive and retain.
The Council of Trent taught that in John 20:22–23 Christ gave the apostles and their successors the power to forgive and retain sins in the sacrament of Penance (Catechism 976, 1441–1442, 1461).
The Sequence.

Veni, Sancte Spiritus, a medieval Latin poem usually attributed to Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury (died 1228), sometimes called the Golden Sequence. It is one of only two sequences that are obligatory in the Roman Rite (with Victimae paschali laudes at Easter).
Red.
The colour of fire and of the martyrs, whose courage was the Spirit's gift. Pentecost is the only Sunday of the Easter season in red.
altar: At every Mass, just before the consecration, the priest extends his hands over the bread and wine and asks the Father to send the Holy Spirit upon them, so that they may become the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. This calling down of the Spirit is called the epiclesis. Without Pentecost there would be no Eucharist.

After the consecration the Church prays a second time for the Spirit, now upon us: that, “filled with his Holy Spirit,” we “may become one body, one spirit in Christ” (Eucharistic Prayer III). Paul's words come true at the altar: “we were all made to drink of one Spirit.”
outline: Light a candle and switch on a fan beside it. Ask: what happens to a flame when the wind blows? Some flames go out; this one, by God's power, spreads.
The Feast of Weeks fulfilled: a new harvest, a new law written on hearts.
Point 2 · Each in their own language
Babel reversed; one Gospel in every tongue.
Point 3 · Varieties of gifts, the same Spirit
Faith itself is his gift; every gift is for the common good.
The breath of new creation, peace and the forgiveness of sins.
Point 5 · With Mary in the upper room
The Mother of the Church at its birth.
The paschal candle carried from the ambo to the font: the Easter fire now burns in the baptised.
“Lord, send forth your Spirit, and renew the face of the earth.”
live: Pray the Veni, Sancte Spiritus slowly today and each day this week, stopping at the line you most need: heal what is wounded, warm what is cold, guide what has gone astray.
Ask yourself, and perhaps a friend: what gift has the Spirit given me for the common good? Then use it this week in your parish or neighbourhood.
The first gift of the risen Lord's breath is forgiveness. If it has been long since your last confession, go this week.
Pentecost is about being understood. Take time to listen to someone who feels unheard, perhaps someone of another language, generation or background, and speak to them in a way they can understand.
Recall the day you were confirmed and the words: Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit. Thank God for it, and ask for a fresh outpouring.
fathers: Where the Church is, there is the Spirit of God; and where the Spirit of God is, there is the Church and every kind of grace.
What the soul is to the human body, the Holy Spirit is to the Body of Christ, which is the Church. If you want to live by the Spirit of Christ, stay in the Body of Christ.

The Spirit is like rain. One and the same rain falls from heaven, yet it becomes white in the lily, red in the rose, purple in the violet. So the one Spirit gives wisdom to one, prophecy to another, and to each as he wills.
Through the Holy Spirit comes our return to paradise, our ascent to the kingdom of heaven, our adoption as children of God, our boldness to call God Father, our share in the grace of Christ.
At Pentecost the Holy Spirit did not begin to work in the saints for the first time; he came with a new fullness, overflowing the measure of earlier gifts.
magis: On the day of Pentecost the Passover of Christ is fulfilled in the outpouring of the Holy Spirit; the Holy Trinity is fully revealed, and the Church is made known to the world.
The Church was made manifest at Pentecost; the Spirit equips her with hierarchical and charismatic gifts.
Confirmation perpetuates the grace of Pentecost in the Church.
The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit and the fruits of the Spirit.
Christ gave the apostles the power to forgive sins: “Receive the Holy Spirit.”
The Spirit was sent on the day of Pentecost to sanctify the Church continually; he dwells in the Church and in the hearts of the faithful as in a temple.
Dominum et Vivificantem 25 (St John Paul II, 1986)
Pentecost is the definitive manifestation of what was accomplished in the Upper Room on Easter Sunday; the era of the Church began with the coming of the Spirit.
saints: The Blessed Virgin Mary in the upper room

The apostles devoted themselves to prayer “together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14). Tradition honours her as Queen of the Apostles. Tomorrow, the Monday after Pentecost, the Church celebrates her as Mother of the Church.

17 May: The Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of the Church (memorial); Ordinary Time resumes (Week 7, Year I). 18 May: St John I, pope and martyr (optional). 20 May: St Bernardine of Siena (optional). 21 May: St Christopher Magallanes and companions (optional). 22 May: St Rita of Cascia (optional). 23 May: The Most Holy Trinity.
2027-05-16.prayer: O God, who by the mystery of today's great feast sanctify your whole Church in every people and nation, pour out, we pray, the gifts of the Holy Spirit across the face of the earth and, with the divine grace that was at work when the Gospel was first proclaimed, fill now once more the hearts of believers. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful and kindle in them the fire of your love. Breath of the risen Christ, give us his peace and the joy of forgiveness. Tongue of fire, give us words to speak of God's deeds of power in every language we know. Giver of gifts, make each of us useful for the common good, and make us one body in Christ. With Mary, who waited with the apostles, we pray: send forth your Spirit, and renew the face of the earth. Amen.

quick: Fifty days after Easter, on the feast of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit came on the disciples with wind and fire, and they spoke so that every nation heard in its own language.
There are varieties of gifts but the same Spirit; no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except by the Spirit, and in one Spirit we were baptised into one body.
On Easter evening the risen Jesus breathed on the apostles: Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven.
2027-05-16.action: Pray the Sequence, Come, Holy Spirit, slowly today, and choose one gift you will use for others this week.
2027-05-16.question: Which room of my life is still behind locked doors, waiting for the Spirit's peace?
catechism: Pentecost: the Passover fulfilled, the Trinity revealed.
Confirmation perpetuates the grace of Pentecost.
The gifts and fruits of the Holy Spirit.
kidsaint: After Jesus went up to heaven, Mary, the Mother of Jesus, prayed with the apostles for nine days, waiting for the Holy Spirit. When the Spirit came like wind and fire, she was there with them. That is why we call her the Mother of the Church. Lesson: when we pray together, like a family with Mary, God gives us his Spirit.
2027-05-16.special: Pentecost Sunday, Year B: Gloria, Sequence (obligatory) and Creed; red vestments; double Alleluia at the dismissal; end of the Easter season; paschal candle moved to the baptistery; from tomorrow the Angelus.
term: From the Greek paraklētos, one called to stand beside you: advocate, helper, comforter. Jesus' name for the Holy Spirit in John 14 to 16. He is “another Advocate,” for Jesus himself is our Advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1).

family.explain: Fifty days after Easter, the friends of Jesus were praying together with Mary. Suddenly there was a noise like a strong wind, and little flames like fire came to rest on each of them. They were filled with the Holy Spirit and were not afraid any more! They went out and spoke about Jesus, and people from many countries understood them in their own language. Today is the birthday of the Church. The same Holy Spirit came to us when we were baptised and confirmed.
family.intention: We pray for all who will be confirmed this year, for our parish, and for people who do not yet know Jesus.
family.ask: Ask: “What good gift has God given to each person in our family?” Let everyone say one gift they see in another. Then pray together: Come, Holy Spirit!

illus: A parish in a Kerala town has Sunday Mass in Malayalam, but after a new factory opened nearby, many workers from Odisha, Jharkhand and Bihar began to come. They stood at the back and understood little. One Pentecost, the youth group asked a young worker to read the Gospel in Hindi after the Malayalam reading, and to lead a prayer of the faithful in his own language. An older parishioner said afterwards: for the first time I understood what Pentecost means. God did not make us all speak one language; he made us one family that listens in many.

pm.open: Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful and kindle in them the fire of your love. Send forth your Spirit, and renew the face of the earth. Amen.
share: All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:4). When have I felt the Spirit give me courage I did not have by myself?
To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good (1 Corinthians 12:7). What is my gift, and am I using it for others?
Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them (John 20:22–23). Is there forgiveness I need to receive, or to give?
pm.resp: Lord, send forth your Spirit, and renew the face of the earth.
interc: For the whole Church on her birthday, that the Holy Spirit may renew her in holiness, unity and missionary courage.
For the Pope, the bishops and all priests, that they may be faithful ministers of the Spirit's forgiveness.
For those preparing for Baptism and Confirmation, that they may open their hearts to the gifts of the Spirit.
For peoples divided by language, caste, race or religion, that the Spirit may help them understand and respect one another.
For the sick, the sad and the discouraged, that the Comforter may console them.
For our group, that each of us may discover and use our gifts for the common good.
pm.close: Father, on this day you sent the Holy Spirit upon the apostles gathered with Mary. Pour out the same Spirit upon us, and make us witnesses of your Son to the ends of the earth. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, happy birthday! Today is the birthday of the Church. Fifty days ago we sang the Alleluia of Easter; today we sing it for the last time in this season, and we celebrate the great gift that Easter was for: the Holy Spirit.

Look at the apostles before Pentecost. They had seen the risen Lord, they had eaten with him, they had watched him ascend. And yet they were still in one room, waiting. Then, when the day of Pentecost had come, suddenly from heaven there came a sound like the rush of a violent wind, and tongues as of fire rested on each of them. All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:2–4). The same frightened men opened the doors and went out into the street to proclaim the deeds of God.

And what happened outside? People from every nation heard them, each in their own native language. At Babel human pride divided languages and scattered people. At Pentecost God's gift gathered them. Notice: the Spirit did not make everyone speak one language. He made the one Gospel understood in many. Here in India we know what that means. In our country the same Mass is offered and the same Gospel proclaimed in many languages, and it is one faith, one Lord, one Spirit.

St Paul tells us that the Spirit is not only for great events. No one can say Jesus is Lord except by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3). Every time you pray, even a simple Jesus, I love you, the Spirit is praying in you. And he gives gifts to each one: there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:4). The gift of teaching, of caring for the sick, of music, of patience with old parents, of making peace. Each is given for the common good. Nobody in the Church is useless; nobody is without a gift.

In the Gospel we go back to Easter evening. The doors are locked; the disciples are afraid. Jesus comes, shows his wounds, and says: Peace be with you. Then he breathed on them and said, Receive the Holy Spirit (John 20:22). Just as God breathed life into Adam at the beginning, the risen Christ breathes new life into his Church. And the first gift of that breath is forgiveness: if you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them. Every confession is a little Pentecost, a breath of new life.

Finally, remember who was in the upper room: Mary, the Mother of Jesus, praying with the apostles. The Spirit who overshadowed her at Nazareth now fills the whole Church. Let us ask her to pray with us today. What doors are locked in our lives? What fears keep us silent? Where do we need forgiveness, healing, warmth? Let us pray with the whole Church: Come, Holy Spirit. Heal what is wounded, warm what is cold, guide what has gone astray. Send forth your Spirit, and renew the face of the earth. Amen. Alleluia, alleluia!
kids: Children, today is the birthday of the Church! Fifty days after Easter, the friends of Jesus were praying with Mary. Suddenly, whoosh, a sound like a strong wind! And little flames like fire came on each of them. It was the Holy Spirit! They were not scared any more, and they told everybody about Jesus.
The Holy Spirit lives in you too, from your Baptism. He helps you pray, be kind and be brave. Let us say together: Come, Holy Spirit, fill my heart with your love!

opts.a: The gifts and the fruit of the Spirit
intro: The Spirit who came at Pentecost comes to each of us in Baptism and Confirmation. He brings gifts that strengthen us and fruit that others can see.

sub: Knowledge, piety, fear of the Lord.
points.apply: Each day this week, ask for one of the seven gifts by name.
Ask a family member which fruit of the Spirit you most need.

sub: Peter and John lay on hands.
points.apply: Find out the date of your Confirmation and pray for your sponsor.

concl: The Spirit gives gifts to make us strong and fruit to make us like Christ.
What began at Pentecost continues in every Confirmation.
opts.resolve: This week I will pray daily for the gifts of the Spirit and work on one fruit of the Spirit.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, at Pentecost the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles with wind and fire. But the Spirit did not come only once, long ago. He comes to every Christian in Baptism and, in a special way, in Confirmation. Today let us look at what he brings: gifts and fruit.

Isaiah foretold the Messiah: the spirit of the LORD shall rest on him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD (Isaiah 11:2). From this passage the Church names seven gifts: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety and fear of the Lord. The Spirit who rested on Christ now rests on us. To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good (1 Corinthians 12:7).

The gifts make us strong. The fruit shows that the Spirit lives in us. Paul writes: the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, generosity, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23). God had promised: I will put my spirit within you (Ezekiel 36:27). If someone wants to know whether the Spirit lives in me, they should not look for wonders but for this fruit. Am I patient? Am I kind? Can I control my tongue?

In the Acts of the Apostles, when the people of Samaria had been baptised, Peter and John came and laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit (Acts 8:17). That is the root of our sacrament of Confirmation. Joel had promised: I will pour out my spirit on all flesh (Joel 2:28). The bishop's hand and the holy chrism seal us with the Spirit, to make us witnesses of Christ.

So today let us thank God for our Confirmation. If you were never confirmed, speak to the parish priest. Pray each day this week for one of the seven gifts. Ask someone at home which fruit you most need, and work on it. And at this Mass, let us pray: Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful. Alleluia. Amen.

opts.a: Father of the poor, best of consolers
intro: Before the Gospel today the Church sings the Golden Sequence, Veni, Sancte Spiritus. It calls the Spirit father of the poor and best of consolers. These titles are a whole teaching on the Spirit.

sub: The Spirit anointed Jesus for the poor.
points.apply: Visit or help one poor person this week in the power of the Spirit.

sub: Rest in labour, comfort in tears.
He stays with us for ever.
points.apply: Console one grieving or lonely person this week.
Before every task this week, pray: Come, Holy Spirit.

concl: The Holy Spirit comes to the poor, consoles the sorrowful and gives life to all.
Without him we can do nothing; with him all things are made new.
opts.resolve: This week I will begin every task with Come, Holy Spirit, and console one person who suffers.
homily: Dear friends, today the Church sings one of her most beautiful prayers, the Golden Sequence: Come, Holy Spirit. It gives the Spirit tender names. Let us reflect on three of them.

First, the Sequence calls him father of the poor. In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus read from Isaiah: the Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor (Luke 4:18; Isaiah 61:1). The Spirit loves to come where hands are empty. The proud and self-sufficient have no room for him. If you feel poor today, in money, in strength, in faith, you are exactly where the Spirit likes to come.

Second, he is called the best of consolers, rest in our labour, coolness in the heat, comfort in our tears. Jesus promised: I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate, to be with you forever (John 14:16). The prophet had heard God say: comfort, O comfort my people (Isaiah 40:1). The Holy Spirit is God's comfort living in us. He does not always take the sorrow away, but he never leaves us alone in it.

Third, the Sequence admits that without the Spirit there is nothing in us, nothing that is not harmful. The psalm says the same: when you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust. When you send forth your spirit, they are created (Psalm 104:29–30). Even our prayer depends on him: the Spirit helps us in our weakness; for we do not know how to pray as we ought (Romans 8:26). Every good thing we do begins with his breath.

So let us make the Sequence our prayer this week. Before every task, say: Come, Holy Spirit. Visit someone poor and console someone in tears, so that through us the Spirit may be father of the poor and consoler of the sorrowful. And at this Mass, let us ask him to send forth his Spirit and renew our hearts. Alleluia, alleluia! Amen.

intro: Theme: “Lord, send forth your Spirit, and renew the face of the earth.”
Pentecost: the wind and fire of Acts 2, the gifts of 1 Corinthians 12, and the breath of the risen Christ on Easter evening.

q: I will put my spirit within you, and you shall live, and I will place you on your own soil; then you shall know that I, the Lord, have spoken and will act, says the Lord.
And suddenly from heaven there came a sound like the rush of a violent wind, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting.
points.apply: Pray each morning this week: Come, Holy Spirit, fill my heart; and ask for the courage to speak of Jesus once each day.

q: Therefore it was called Babel, because there the Lord confused the language of all the earth; and from there the Lord scattered them abroad over the face of all the earth.
And at this sound the crowd gathered and was bewildered, because each one heard them speaking in the native language of each.
points.apply: Reach out this week to someone of another language or background in your parish or workplace, and make them feel at home.

points.h: Varieties of gifts, the same Spirit
q: Then afterward I will pour out my spirit on all flesh; your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions.
Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit;
points.apply: Name one gift you have received and offer it to your parish this month: in the choir, catechism, care for the sick or the poor.

q: A new heart I will give you, and a new spirit I will put within you; and I will remove from your body the heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh.
When he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit.
points.apply: Go to confession before the end of this month, and forgive one person from your heart.

concl: Pentecost fulfils Easter: the risen Christ pours out the Spirit who makes the Church one, holy and sent.
The same Spirit who came upon Mary and the apostles lives in us by Baptism and Confirmation, gives each of us gifts, and breathes forgiveness into the world.
2027-05-16.resolve: Pray the Sequence Come, Holy Spirit each day this week, and put one gift of the Spirit to work for the common good.
